newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Paper capers.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Paper capers.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
Funny things tend to happen when politicians upset media moguls. Just ask Paul Keating.
Now, John Howard's finding out too.

"Missing in action" was the headline on a Malcolm Farr feature in Rupert Murdoch's Daily Telegraph on Monday. The article itself spoke of "a collapse of leadership" and "dithering, indecision and timidity".

Worse for the prime minister was to come in Piers Ackerman's column on Tuesday which dubbed Kerry Packer "porn to rule" and admonished Howard to "show strength of character" and resist Packer's bid to have the cross media rules dumped so he could take over the Fairfax newspaper empire.
Why are prime minister's attracted to fiddling with media ownership like bees to a honey pot? It obsessed Fraser, Hawke and Keating and now it's got Howard too.
Influence is what it's all about -- and power too -- but inevitably it leads to trouble as well.

The government may not think it matters much to the battlers, but, even at the margin, all the wheeling, dealing and meetings in the 90s equivalent of smoke filled rooms looks a little tacky and sits uneasily with Howard's claim to be a break with the past -- to have higher standards than his Labor predecessors and their "mates."

A more serious point of principle comes with the spectacle of a prime minister actively canvassing the break up of a public company and now apparently contemplating an outcome clearly designed to hit one company.

In this case, it's Fairfax, with thought turning to a change of the rules to force any future owner (read Packer) to divest one of the group's newspapers by forbidding a future proprietor with television interests to own more than one newspaper in a capital city.
It's no different from Paul Keating's push in the 1980s for the cross media rules to wreak vengeance on the Herald and Weekly Times in the 1980s.
The Howard cabinet may be keen to move, not so his backbench which can't see how an end to the cross media rules will aid diversity and have been saying so publicly.
So much so that they're to be briefed -- apparently in advance of any established cabinet option.
That's generally a sign that a decision is to be delayed.
If a leader wants to advance a difficult decision the strategy is to lock in the frontbench -- then consult the backbench.
Which brings us to Wik.
Without doubt, Native Title has been Howard's toughest problem.
It was, too, for Paul Keating.
To the point where it overwhelmed the rest of the decision making process -- and added to the Labor government's popularity to boot.
Now that boot's on the other foot.
For all the National party's bluster the signs are that they know the prime minister will prevail.
His 10 point plan should pass the joint party room next week, but there will be collateral damage for Howard.
The National Party will be more embittered than ever.
The gun bans and buyback in the wake of Port Arthur marked the beginning of the serious strains between the coalition partners.
Wik has taken the Liberal-National marriage close to divorce.
They will patch it up, but Tim Fischer could well lose his leadership.
Not immediately.
The Nationals are always keen on decent intervals.
However, Wik has shown Fischer to be impotent on a "core" National party issue.
Howard has not just ridden rough shod over the man he calls his magnificently loyal deputy this week, he humiliated him.
Fischer contributed to his troubles.

His problem was that he went to the wrong meeting. He should have stayed away from the Nationals management committee meeting, given it was always certain to come up with a stand Howard and the Liberal dominated cabinet would reject.
Fischer should have gone to the cabinet meeting which endorsed the Howard 10 point plan. He would still have lost, but he would have been able to argue he'd forcefully put the Nationals case.
Instead, he was out on a limb in Brisbane when the prime minister withdrew his brief permit for Fischer to have a holiday from cabinet solidarity.
It left Fischer with nowhere to go and no base from which to argue convincingly that he'd done everything to advance the Nationals cause.
Now, all the Nationals are left to do is build up a few brownie points with their constituency before Howard formally rolls over them at next week's joint party meeting.
A good outcome, but the lead work has been flawed to say the least and definitely not an example of powerful leadership on Howard's part.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
